title: Size-Dependent Growth Rates Amplify Infinitesimal Asymmetry in Nanocrystals
abstract: The kinetic Wulff construction predicts symmetric nonequilibrium shapes when crystallographically equivalent facets share a fixed growth rate. However, nanocrystals grow through finite facets whose nucleation barriers and ligand coverages depend on facet size. Here we develop a size-dependent kinetic construction and show that as a consequence infinitesimal seed asymmetries can be amplified into strongly asymmetric nanocrystal morphologies even when all symmetry-related facets obey the same microscopic growth law. Spatially heterogeneous nucleation rates and boundary limited growth generate facet growth velocities that depend on size, and deterministic shape evolution translates these local rates into global shape symmetry breaking. We illustrate the mechanism of persistent anisotropic growth on square and triangular lattices in two dimensions and on FCC seeds in three dimensions, where cuboctahedra can evolve toward rods or tetrahedra depending on which facet-area perturbations are amplified.
summary: This paper introduces a size-dependent kinetic construction to model nanocrystal growth, moving beyond symmetry-preserving assumptions. By showing that facet growth rates depend on the facet's size, the authors demonstrate that even tiny initial asymmetries can be amplified into large, macroscopic shape anisotropies. This mechanism is crucial for understanding how crystal morphology is determined by local, size-sensitive kinetic processes.
main_problem: To develop a predictive theory explaining how infinitesimal initial asymmetries in nanocrystals can be amplified into strongly asymmetric morphologies, overcoming the symmetry constraints of traditional growth models.
main_result: Size-dependent kinetic growth rates, arising from finite facet effects, cause deterministic shape evolution to amplify small perturbations, leading to macroscopic shape symmetry breaking.
method: The authors developed a size-dependent kinetic construction generalizing the Wulff construction, using probabilistic lattice gas models to derive facet growth velocities dependent on facet size.
model_or_system: The study models the growth of nanocrystals (e.g., on square, triangular, or FCC lattices) where facet growth rates are governed by local nucleation barriers and ligand coverages that vary with the instantaneous facet size.
key_observables: Facet growth velocities ($V_\alpha(D)$), shape asymmetry measures ($A_{2d}, A_{3d}$), and the evolution of crystal morphology (e.g., cuboctahedra to rods).
important_parameters: Facet size ($D$), ligand coverage ($ho_l$), and the crossover areas ($A_{c,\alpha}$) where growth kinetics change significantly.
main_assumptions: The theory assumes ligands equilibrate quickly, allowing the facet state to switch between ligand-poor and ligand-rich regimes, and the growth is deterministic based on derived rate laws.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the microscopic origin of size-dependent velocities, show the instability of symmetric growth on 2D lattices, and demonstrate the amplification of small seed perturbations into highly anisotropic 3D rod shapes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the limitations of the standard kinetic Wulff construction to developing the size-dependent kinetic construction using a lattice gas model. It then applies this theory to 2D and 3D systems, showing how size-dependent rates lead to shape instability and macroscopic asymmetry amplification.
why_interesting: The concept of size-dependent, non-linear kinetics leading to symmetry breaking is highly relevant to non-equilibrium dynamics, pattern formation, and the study of open quantum systems where boundary effects or finite size corrections become crucial.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Microscopic origin of facet-area-dependent growth velocities. Left, normalized layer-completion times, τ/maxrτ, for finite square {100} and hexagonal {111} facets with A = 50a2 and 900a2 using corner, edge, and interior nucleation rates obtained from the ligand-renormalized microscopic attachment/removal rates. Right, dimensionless velocities Vα(A)/(ak0) for the same facet families. Solid black curves include ligand blocking, dashed black curves show the corresponding ligand-free velocities, and blue curves show the mean ligand density ρl. In all panels a = 1, k0 = 1, βϵn = 5, and βϵl = 4. For {100} facets, z100 = 2, β∆µn = 7, and β∆µl = 1. For {111} facets, z111 = 3, β∆µn = 12, and...

FIG. 2. Area-normalized two-dimensional shape evolution un- der the size-dependent velocity law. Rows show (a) a square seed with Lx = Ly = 7a, (b) a rectangular square-lattice seed with Lx = 6a and Ly = 7a, (c) an ideal triangular-lattice hexagon, (d) a triangular seed with a single-facet perturba- tion, (e) a triangular seed with opposite-facet perturbations, and (f) a triangular seed with adjacent-facet perturbations. The time slices are logarithmically spaced after t = 0, and each polygon is centered and rescaled to its initial area.

FIG. 3. Shape and size trajectories for the six cases in Fig. 2. The upper panel shows the shape asymmetry, and the lower panel shows the crystal area relative to its initial area. Legend labels correspond to the snapshot rows.

FIG. 4. FCC shape evolution for the global rod comparison. Rows show (a) the unperturbed {111}-threshold regime, (b) the unperturbed {100}-threshold regime, (c) a single {111} perturbation, (d) opposing {111} perturbations, (e) adjacent {111} perturbations, (f) a single {100} perturbation, (g) op- posing {100} perturbations, and (h) adjacent {100} pertur- bations. Time increases from left to right. Each polyhedron is centered and rescaled independently for visualization.

FIG. 5. Sensitivity of FCC rod formation to seed perturbation and crossover area. The left column shows the {100}-faceted rod parameter set, and the right column shows the {111}- faceted rod parameter set. (a,b) Initial and final volume- weighted asymmetry as a function of perturbation height δh. (c,d) Final asymmetry as a function of the relevant crossover area at fixed δh = a. Dashed vertical lines mark the sur- viving facet areas at which the complementary facet family disappears during rod formation.
